title: Six Months Coding With AI: The Unhyped Version
author: Sarath Kumar
summary: What actually changed after six months of building with AI agents — the rules files, the five-stage workflow, the security traps nobody warns you about, and the one habit that matters most.
content: Six months ago I started doing most of my engineering work alongside an AI agent. This is the unhyped version of what I learned — not the demo-day version. The short of it: I'm still the engineer. The AI never was. What changed is the rhythm of the work, not who's accountable for it.

My day used to start with a ticket, six browser tabs, and a hunt through Teams and Confluence for context. Forty minutes gone before I wrote a single line — then I'd do it again for the next ticket. The same role looks completely different now. I type less and read more. I spend my attention on what to build instead of how to spell it. That shift sounds small; in practice it's most of the gain.

The first thing worth setting up is the rules file every agent reads the second it starts — AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, whatever your tool calls it. Inside go the things that are always true: your stack, your conventions, what to never touch, how to test, your branch strategy. Anything that's only true some of the time doesn't belong here — that's what a skill is for. Two lines from mine do a lot of work: 'Fix X means fix X — don't widen scope,' and 'keep it under ~150 lines.' Keep the file team-only; personal preferences belong in your own user config, not the shared one.

Three concepts took me embarrassingly long to stop mixing up. A skill is knowledge the agent pulls in automatically when a task needs it — reach for one when you keep hitting the same kind of problem. A subagent is a worker that does heavy lifting in its own separate context and reports back — reach for one when there's a lot to read but only a small answer to return. A slash command is just a saved prompt you fire with /name — reach for one when you notice you're typing the same instruction twice.

Then there's MCP — the protocol that lets agents reach outside the chat to Jira, GitHub, your database, your files. If you're copy-pasting from a tool into your agent, there's probably an MCP for it. What's connected determines what the agent can actually do, not just what it knows; mine pulls Jira tickets directly so I never summarize them by hand. But watch the doors. Every connection is one more thing that can be misused, so treat enabling one like installing a new package: review what it can do before you flip it on.

The most counterintuitive lesson is that long chats don't make agents smarter — they make them worse, and well before any token limit. When an agent starts drifting mid-session, it's almost always the context, not the model. Three fixes actually move the needle for me: let subagents do the reading so the report comes back clean and the main chat stays focused; run /clear between unrelated tasks so a new problem gets a fresh head; and keep a plan document the agent can re-read as a cheap save point.

Picking the model is its own small discipline. Cheap and fast is right for poking around, edits, boilerplate, and refactors I could do myself. Slow and expensive is for planning a feature, hard debugging, anything architectural. I start with the fast option and only switch up when it gets stuck. Pick wrong in either direction and you're either bleeding money or waiting forever.

AI also quietly changed what I have to worry about on security — both what leaves my machine and what comes back to it. Going out: I never paste secrets, customer data, unreleased code, or anything internal. Tool-approved is not content-approved; the policy is about what you send, not which vendor receives it. Coming in: AI sometimes invents package names, and attackers register those exact names with malware attached — it's common enough to have a label, slopsquatting. So I treat AI output like a pull request from someone I don't know: scan it, test it, read it.

Which is the real headline. The AI is a fast junior, not a senior. It multiplies me — which means it multiplies my mistakes too. Three things I've watched it do with full confidence: give a flatly wrong answer as if it were certain, invent an API that doesn't exist, and make a failing test pass by quietly deleting it. So I read everything it writes and verify everything it claims, every single time. If you take one thing from this, take that one.

The structure that makes all of this reliable is a five-stage loop I run every time: Setup, Triage, Verify, Plan, Execute. The trick is that every stage produces a document, and the next stage starts from that document. The documents are the workflow — not the chat, and not whatever I'm holding in my head.

Setup and triage are where a new task begins: a skill grabs the Jira ticket and surrounding context, and the agent drafts a quick investigation doc into a project folder I keep for exactly this. What comes back is the AI's first guess at what's actually going on. I read it as a map, not as the answer.

Verify is the stage almost everyone skips, and it's the one that matters most. Before I believe anything, I reproduce the bug myself. I open the files the AI pointed at and actually read them — not skim. And if I disagree with what it wrote, I write that disagreement straight into the doc. Nothing moves forward until I've done all three.

Plan is a numbered list of every step — code changes and tests, no exceptions — written so any agent in any new session can pick up exactly where I left off. That one document solves three problems at once: context rot, because the plan gets re-read every session; the 'wait, what was I doing again' tax; and handing the work off, whether to another agent or another person. When the agent starts drifting, I rewrite the plan. I never just push through.

If you're starting your own setup, don't copy mine — build one that's actually yours. Frontend, backend, data, and infra each need different rules and different skills. Start with the bare minimum that works for you, and don't add a rule until something has broken twice. The goal isn't to imitate someone else's config; it's to end up with a setup you understand and trust.

Where this is heading is more of the same fundamentals, formalized: spec-driven development with tools like Spec Kit, Kiro, and BMAD; async and cloud agents you hand a ticket and come back to a finished PR; design-to-code pipelines that turn a prompt into UI and code; and uses well beyond coding entirely. The tools will keep changing. The one habit underneath them won't: read everything it writes, verify everything it claims, every time.
